laws.fullDescription: NSW's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) has been one of Australia's most active anti-corruption bodies, exposing corrupt conduct by politicians, public servants, and others. Former Premiers such as Barry O'Farrell resigned after ICAC findings (though corruption not found). The QLD Crime and Corruption Commission and WA Corruption and Crime Commission have also made significant findings. ICAC's powers to hold public hearings has been controversial.
laws.penalty: ICAC findings can lead to criminal prosecution; politicians may face sanctions including disqualification
exceptions: ICAC cannot make criminal findings — refers to prosecutors
Procedural fairness applies to ICAC processes

quiz.q: What was the outcome for NSW Premier Barry O'Farrell following ICAC proceedings?
options: He resigned after being caught in an error about a bottle of wine
He won defamation proceedings against ICAC
quiz.explanation: Barry O'Farrell resigned as NSW Premier in 2014 after ICAC revealed he had forgotten receiving a bottle of Penfolds Grange wine (valued at ~$3,000) from a lobbyist and had provided incorrect evidence to ICAC, even though corruption was not ultimately found.

laws.title: National Recovery Plans / Bushfire Response
laws.subtitle: Post-bushfire recovery law and climate adaptation
laws.fullDescription: The 2019-20 Black Summer bushfires, which burned over 18 million hectares and destroyed 3,000+ homes, prompted the establishment of the National Recovery and Resilience Agency (NRRA). The subsequent Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements led to reforms in federal emergency powers, cross-border coordination, and Commonwealth involvement in disaster response. Australia's disaster costs are projected to reach AU$39 billion annually by 2050.
laws.penalty: Arson causing bushfires: up to 25 years imprisonment in some states; illegal burning: significant fines
exceptions: Controlled burns with permit
Indigenous cultural burns increasingly recognized

quiz.q: How many hectares did Australia's 2019-20 Black Summer bushfires burn?
quiz.explanation: Australia's 2019-20 Black Summer bushfires burned approximately 18.6 million hectares, destroyed over 3,000 homes, and killed an estimated 3 billion animals in one of the worst fire seasons in recorded history.

laws.title: Senate Voting Reform 2016
laws.subtitle: Optional preferential above-the-line voting
laws.fullDescription: The 2016 Senate voting reforms replaced group voting tickets (which allowed obscure parties to direct preferences without voter knowledge) with optional preferential above-the-line voting. Voters can now number at least 6 boxes above the line (for parties) or 12 below the line (for individual candidates). This led to the 'teals' and independents gaining more influence in the Senate and the 2022 election saw a record crossbench.
laws.penalty: False declarations on enrolment: criminal penalties; misleading electoral material: electoral offenses
exceptions: Donkey votes are informal only if no candidates are numbered
Overseas voters have special voting arrangements

quiz.q: What minimum number of boxes must voters number above the line in Australian Senate elections after the 2016 reform?
quiz.explanation: After the 2016 Senate voting reform, voters must number at least 6 boxes above the line (for parties/groups) to cast a formal vote, replacing the old single-box group voting ticket system.

laws.title: Critical Minerals Strategy
laws.subtitle: Lithium, cobalt and strategic resources
laws.fullDescription: Australia holds the world's largest reserves of many critical minerals including lithium (largest), cobalt, nickel, and rare earths. The Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030 aims to value-add minerals onshore rather than exporting raw ore. Australia has partnered with the US, EU, Japan, and South Korea to supply critical minerals away from Chinese-dominated supply chains. The METS Ignited cluster and government subsidies aim to develop downstream processing.
laws.penalty: Export controls on critical minerals being developed; unauthorized export: criminal penalties
exceptions: Existing supply contracts continue under transition arrangements
Allied nation preferential access frameworks

quiz.q: What is Australia's ranking among global holders of lithium reserves?
quiz.explanation: Australia holds the world's largest lithium reserves, and is also the largest lithium producer, making it a strategically crucial supplier for electric vehicle batteries and energy storage.

laws.title: Residential Tenancy Laws / Rental Crisis
laws.subtitle: Tenant rights amid rental affordability crisis
laws.fullDescription: Residential tenancy law in Australia is state-based, creating significant variation in tenant protections. Australia faces a severe rental crisis — national median rents surged 30%+ between 2020 and 2024, vacancy rates fell to historic lows, and homelessness increased. Policy debates center on no-cause eviction bans (adopted in some states), rent increase limits, and minimum rental standards for heating, cooling, and insulation.
laws.penalty: Illegal evictions: state tribunal orders for reinstatement; fines for landlord violations
exceptions: Fixed-term tenancies have different notice requirements
Rooming houses and co-tenancies have modified rules

quiz.q: Approximately how much did Australian median rents increase between 2020 and 2024?
quiz.explanation: Australian median rents increased by more than 30% between 2020 and 2024, driven by low vacancy rates, population growth, and reduced housing supply, creating one of Australia's worst rental affordability crises.

laws.title: Open Banking / Consumer Data Right
laws.subtitle: CDR and financial data portability
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Consumer Data Right (CDR), introduced from 2020, gives consumers the right to request that their data be shared with accredited third parties ('open banking'). Starting with banking and expanding to energy and telecommunications, the CDR aims to increase competition and innovation. Australia is among the first countries globally to implement a cross-sector CDR framework.
laws.penalty: Data holders that fail to comply with CDR: fines up to AU$10 million; ACCC enforcement
exceptions: CDR only applies to accredited data recipients
Privacy protections limit how shared data can be used

quiz.q: What does CDR stand for in Australian data law?
quiz.explanation: CDR stands for Consumer Data Right, Australia's framework (from 2020) giving consumers the right to access and share their own data with accredited parties, starting with banking and extending to other sectors.

laws.title: Euthanasia to VAD / Abortion Law Reforms
laws.subtitle: Reproductive rights and abortion law
laws.fullDescription: Abortion law in Australia is state-based and has been progressively decriminalized. NSW decriminalized abortion in 2019, the last mainland state to do so. SA decriminalized in 2021. Western Australia has had decriminalization since 1998. The ACT and Victoria have the most liberal frameworks with abortion available up to 24 weeks without restriction. Safe access zones around clinics prevent harassment.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized late-term abortion: criminal penalties in some states; harassing patients in safe zones: fines
exceptions: Emergency medical procedures protecting the mother's life
Medical practitioners have conscientious objection rights but must refer
laws.sourceLabel: Medical Journal of Australia Abortion Law

quiz.q: Which Australian state was the last mainland state to decriminalize abortion?
quiz.explanation: New South Wales was the last Australian mainland state to decriminalize abortion, passing the Abortion Law Reform Act 2019 under Premier Gladys Berejiklian, over 20 years after Western Australia first decriminalized.

laws.title: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act
laws.subtitle: SOCI Act and cyber resilience
laws.fullDescription: The Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018, significantly expanded in 2022, requires operators of critical infrastructure (energy, water, communications, finance, transport, food, health, defence, space) to report cyber incidents and implement risk management programs. The ACSC can provide 'last resort' government assistance during cyber attacks. The 2022 Optus and Medibank breaches accelerated further reforms.
laws.penalty: Failure to comply with SOCI obligations: civil penalties up to AU$11 million; criminal penalties for deliberate obstruction
exceptions: Small entities below defined thresholds
Intelligence agencies have separate frameworks

quiz.q: How many critical infrastructure sectors does the expanded SOCI Act 2022 cover?
quiz.explanation: The Security of Critical Infrastructure Act, expanded in 2022, covers at least 11 critical infrastructure sectors including energy, water, communications, finance, transport, food, health, defence, space, education, and research.

laws.title: Wage Theft Laws
laws.subtitle: Criminalization of employer underpayment
laws.fullDescription: Several Australian states criminalized wage theft — deliberate underpayment of workers — in the late 2010s and early 2020s (Victoria first in 2021, QLD following). The federal Closing Loopholes Act 2023 introduced a national criminal offense for intentional wage theft from 2025. Australia has an estimated AU$1.35 billion in wage theft annually. High-profile cases included 7-Eleven franchisees, Coles, Woolworths, and Commonwealth Bank underpaying workers.
laws.penalty: Intentional wage theft: up to 10 years imprisonment; civil penalties for inadvertent underpayment
exceptions: Genuine mistakes not covered by criminal provisions
Companies that self-report receive cooperation credit

quiz.q: In what year did Victoria become the first Australian state to criminalize wage theft?
quiz.explanation: Victoria became the first Australian state to criminalize wage theft in 2021, with other states and eventually the Commonwealth following with national criminal wage theft provisions from 2025.

laws.title: Australia in International Law / AUKUS and ICJ
laws.subtitle: International law obligations and disputes
laws.fullDescription: Australia is a party to major international conventions and has been involved in landmark International Court of Justice cases, including East Timor v Australia (1995) and Whaling in the Antarctic (2014), where Australia successfully challenged Japan's 'scientific' whaling program. AUKUS raises international law questions around nuclear non-proliferation and the NPT submarine exception. Australia is active in international human rights treaty bodies.
laws.penalty: No direct domestic penalties for international law violations; diplomatic consequences
exceptions: National security exceptions in many treaties
Australia can derogate from some ICCPR rights in emergencies

quiz.q: In what ICJ case did Australia successfully challenge Japan's Antarctic whaling program?
quiz.explanation: In Whaling in the Antarctic (Australia v Japan) 2014, the International Court of Justice ruled in Australia's favor, finding Japan's so-called 'scientific' whaling program in the Antarctic was not scientific in nature and ordering it to cease.

laws.title: Teal Independents / Voices for
laws.subtitle: 2022 election and crossbench rise
laws.fullDescription: The 2022 Australian federal election saw a record crossbench elected to the House of Representatives, including 6 'teal' independents (climate-focused, professionally-credentialed women) who defeated sitting Liberal MPs in traditionally safe seats. The Greens won 12 Senate seats. This shifted power dynamics significantly — the Albanese Labor government governs with a crossbench that includes the Greens, teals, and other independents, creating unusual legislative dynamics.
laws.penalty: Campaign finance disclosure obligations; election advertising disclosure requirements
exceptions: Electoral pendulum can return seats to major parties
Redistributions affect electorate boundaries

quiz.q: How many 'teal' independent MPs were elected in Australia's 2022 federal election?
quiz.explanation: Six 'teal' independent MPs were elected in Australia's 2022 federal election, defeating sitting Liberal MPs in traditionally safe seats in inner-city and coastal electorates by running on climate action and integrity platforms.

laws.title: Net Zero by 2050 / Offshore Wind
laws.subtitle: Offshore wind legislation and renewables
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Offshore Electricity Infrastructure Act 2021 created the framework for offshore wind energy, with major projects proposed off Victoria (Gippsland), NSW, and other states. Australia has among the world's best renewable resources — wind, solar, and hydro. The Capacity Investment Scheme tenders are driving private investment. Australia is targeting 82% renewable electricity by 2030 and has committed to net zero by 2050 under the Climate Change Act 2022.
laws.penalty: Offshore infrastructure without license: criminal penalties; environmental conditions violations: regulatory sanctions
exceptions: Existing offshore oil and gas operations continue under separate framework
State waters vs Commonwealth waters have jurisdictional differences

quiz.q: What percentage of electricity does Australia's Capacity Investment Scheme target from renewables by 2030?
quiz.explanation: Australia is targeting 82% renewable electricity by 2030 through the Capacity Investment Scheme and other policy mechanisms, a significant increase from the approximately 35% renewable share when the target was set.

laws.title: Opioid Crisis / Prescription Regulation
laws.subtitle: OxyContin and prescription drug abuse
laws.fullDescription: Australia faced a significant opioid crisis in the 2010s, linked to over-prescription of opioids including OxyContin. The TGA strengthened scheduling controls on opioids, requiring real-time prescription monitoring (RTPM) across all states by 2020. Australia also legalized low-dose codeine products by prescription only (previously available OTC) in 2018. The ongoing challenge is balancing adequate pain management with preventing addiction and diversion.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed drug supply including opioids: up to life imprisonment for commercial quantities
exceptions: Palliative care has specific provisions for higher opioid doses
Opioid agonist therapy (methadone, buprenorphine) is regulated separately

quiz.q: What change did Australia make to low-dose codeine products in 2018?
quiz.explanation: In 2018, Australia moved low-dose codeine-containing products (such as Nurofen Plus and Panadeine) from over-the-counter availability to prescription-only, to address misuse and addiction associated with these products.

laws.title: Whistleblower Protection / Treasury Laws
laws.subtitle: Whistleblower protections in corporate law
laws.fullDescription: The Treasury Laws Amendment (Enhancing Whistleblower Protections) Act 2019 strengthened corporate whistleblower protections, requiring large companies to have whistleblower policies. Whistleblowers can disclose to ASIC, APRA, and other regulators with protection from civil, criminal, and administrative liability. The public interest disclosure provisions allow certain disclosures to journalists or politicians after notification to the entity.
laws.penalty: Victimizing a whistleblower: civil penalties up to AU$1 million for individuals
exceptions: Disclosures that are not made in good faith not protected
ASIO and intelligence agencies have different frameworks

quiz.q: What must large companies do regarding whistleblowing under the 2019 Treasury Laws Amendment?
quiz.explanation: The Treasury Laws Amendment (Enhancing Whistleblower Protections) Act 2019 requires large private companies and public companies to have a written whistleblower policy, and to make it available to officers and employees.

laws.title: Digital Platform Services Inquiry / Big Tech
laws.subtitle: ACCC digital platform regulation
laws.fullDescription: The ACCC's Digital Platform Services Inquiry (2020-2025) examines competition, consumer protection, and media impacts of Google, Apple, Facebook/Meta, and other platforms. Australia's Digital Markets Act proposals (2024) would designate 'designated digital platform services' with specific obligations including interoperability and data access. The News Media Bargaining Code (NMBC) was the first legislation globally to require platforms to pay publishers.
laws.penalty: Breaching digital platform obligations: fines up to AU$50 million; ACCC enforcement
exceptions: Small platforms below user thresholds not designated
Australian-owned platforms may have different treatment

quiz.q: What global first did Australia's News Media Bargaining Code achieve?
options: First legislation requiring tech platforms to pay news publishers
First country to tax advertising revenue of tech giants
quiz.explanation: Australia's News Media Bargaining Code (2021) was the first legislation in the world to require digital platforms (Google and Meta) to negotiate and pay news publishers for using their content, inspiring similar legislation in Canada, the EU, and elsewhere.

laws.title: Defence Act 1903 / AUKUS Submarine Program
laws.subtitle: Defence procurement and AUKUS
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Defence Act 1903 and the Defence Force Discipline Act govern the Australian Defence Force (ADF). AUKUS — the trilateral security partnership with the US and UK announced in 2021 — represents Australia's largest-ever defence procurement: nuclear-powered (but conventionally armed) submarines. Costs are estimated at AU$300-368 billion by 2055. Australia is also investing in long-range missiles, cyber capabilities, and autonomous systems under the Defence Strategic Review (2023).
laws.penalty: Military offenses under DFDA: court martial; civilian contractors: standard criminal law
exceptions: Defence cooperation with allied nations has broad exemptions from standard procurement rules
Classified programs have reduced public disclosure

quiz.q: What is the estimated cost of Australia's AUKUS nuclear submarine program by 2055?
quiz.explanation: Australia's AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine program is estimated to cost between AU$300 billion and AU$368 billion by 2055, making it the largest and most expensive defence acquisition in Australian history.

laws.title: Child Support / Family Court Reform 2023
laws.subtitle: Child support and family law modernization
laws.fullDescription: Australia's child support system (Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989) calculates maintenance based on both parents' incomes and the care percentage for each child. The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA), established in 2021 by merging the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, handles family law matters. The 2023 Family Law Amendment Act removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility that critics said exposed children to domestic violence.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of child support: garnishment of wages; contempt of court for order violations
exceptions: Special circumstance departures from formula
International cases under Hague Convention on Child Abduction
laws.sourceLabel: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia

quiz.q: What presumption did the 2023 Family Law Amendment Act remove from Australian law?
options: The presumption of innocent until proven guilty in family matters
The presumption of equal shared parental responsibility
The presumption that mothers should have primary custody
The presumption that courts should prefer mediation to litigation
quiz.explanation: The 2023 Family Law Amendment Act removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility, which critics had argued was being applied in ways that exposed children to ongoing contact with domestically violent parents.

laws.title: Land Rights Act NT / ATSIC History
laws.subtitle: Aboriginal land rights in the Northern Territory
laws.fullDescription: The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 granted Aboriginal Australians freehold title to about 50% of the NT. The NT Intervention (National Emergency Response) 2007, framed as a response to child abuse, controversially suspended the Racial Discrimination Act and imposed welfare quarantining, alcohol restrictions, and compulsory acquisition of Aboriginal communities. The Closing the Gap strategy aims to address outcomes without such coercive approaches.
laws.penalty: Trespassing on Aboriginal land without permit: criminal offense
exceptions: Mining rights complex — ALT must negotiate with companies
Public access to beaches and rivers maintained in some areas

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of the Northern Territory has Aboriginal land rights under the 1976 Act?
quiz.explanation: The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 granted Aboriginal Australians freehold title to approximately 50% of the Northern Territory, with land trusts holding the title for Aboriginal communities.

laws.title: Emergency Management Act / COVID-19 Response
laws.subtitle: State emergency powers and pandemic law
laws.fullDescription: Australia's pandemic response was primarily managed under state and territory public health and emergency management legislation. State Chief Health Officers issued unprecedented public health directions — mandatory vaccination for workers, lockdowns, mask mandates, and border closures. Victoria had the world's longest lockdowns (over 260 days total). Legal challenges to these measures were largely unsuccessful, with courts deferring to public health expertise.
laws.penalty: Violating public health directions during emergencies: fines up to AU$5,000-$25,000 for individuals
exceptions: Exemptions issued for essential workers
Medical exemptions for vaccination requirements

quiz.q: How many total days of lockdown did Victoria experience during the COVID-19 pandemic — the longest in the world?
quiz.explanation: Victoria experienced over 260 days of COVID-19 lockdowns in total — the longest cumulative lockdown period of any city in the world — under the direction of the Victorian Chief Health Officer.

laws.title: Stage 3 Tax Cuts / Income Tax Reform
laws.subtitle: Income tax reform and redistribution
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Stage 3 tax cuts, legislated under the Morrison government (2018), were set to flatten income tax rates and benefit high earners from 2024. The Albanese government controversially redesigned the cuts in 2024 — redirecting more benefit to middle and low earners — breaking a pre-election commitment but arguing it was fairer given changed economic circumstances. The redesign passed with cross-bench support and was upheld as constitutionally valid.
laws.penalty: Income tax evasion: significant criminal penalties; ATO penalties up to 90% of tax owed
exceptions: Low income tax offset (LITO) reduces effective tax for low earners
Senior and disability tax offsets

quiz.q: What did the Albanese government do with the Stage 3 tax cuts in 2024?
options: Redesigned them to benefit middle and low earners more
quiz.explanation: The Albanese government redesigned the Stage 3 tax cuts in 2024 to redirect more of the benefit to middle and low-income earners, breaking a pre-election commitment but arguing the changed economic circumstances (inflation) justified the restructuring.

laws.title: Supermarket Inquiry / Grocery Prices
laws.subtitle: Coles, Woolworths and market concentration
laws.fullDescription: Australia's grocery market is dominated by Coles and Woolworths ('the duopoly'), with a combined market share of approximately 65%. The ACCC's 2024 Supermarket Inquiry examined allegations of price gouging, below-cost selling to drive out independent retailers, and misuse of market power. The Senate also held an inquiry. Independent grocers, including Aldi and IGA, play a role but competition concerns are ongoing.
laws.penalty: Misuse of market power: ACCC civil penalties; predatory pricing: potential enforcement action
exceptions: Collective bargaining by farmers negotiating with supermarkets permitted
Formal price monitoring during emergencies

quiz.q: What is the approximate combined market share of Coles and Woolworths in Australian grocery retail?
quiz.explanation: Coles and Woolworths together hold approximately 65% of Australia's grocery market, making the 'duopoly' one of the most concentrated grocery markets among comparable economies.

laws.title: Online Safety Commissioner / Image-Based Abuse
laws.subtitle: eSafety and harmful online content
laws.fullDescription: Australia's eSafety Commissioner — the world's first such government role — has powers under the Online Safety Act 2021 to require removal of harmful online content including adult cyber abuse, image-based abuse ('revenge porn'), child sexual abuse material, and violent extremist content. The eSafety Commissioner has been active in international forums and has issued notices to major platforms including Twitter/X. Australia has been a global leader in online safety regulation.
laws.penalty: Platforms failing to comply with eSafety removal notices: fines up to AU$782,500 per day
exceptions: Law enforcement access to CSAM evidence under court order
Academic research with appropriate ethics approval

quiz.q: What makes Australia's eSafety Commissioner historically significant?
options: It is the world's strictest media regulator
It was the world's first government online safety role
It has the highest fines in the world for platform non-compliance
It is the only regulator that can shut down websites
quiz.explanation: Australia's eSafety Commissioner, established under the Online Safety Act 2021 (building on earlier legislation), was the world's first government online safety role, with powers to require removal of harmful online content.

laws.title: Referendum on the Republic / Monarchy
laws.subtitle: Australian republicanism and constitutional status
laws.fullDescription: Australia is a constitutional monarchy with King Charles III (since 2022) as head of state, represented by the Governor-General. The 1999 republic referendum was defeated 55-45 against the proposed model (a president elected by parliament, not directly by the people). Australian republican advocates continue to push for a new referendum on a directly elected president model. Support for a republic polls between 40-55% depending on the question asked.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; constitutional and political consequences
exceptions: Republic would require referendum — states and territory majority required
Existing governor-general powers would transfer to president

quiz.q: What was the result of Australia's 1999 republic referendum?
quiz.explanation: Australia's 1999 republic referendum was defeated by 55-45 against the proposed republic model (a president appointed by parliament), partly because many republicans also wanted a directly elected president.

laws.title: Temporary Skill Shortage Visa / Migration Review
laws.subtitle: Skilled migration and TSS visas
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Temporary Skill Shortage (TSS) visa (subclass 482) replaced the 457 visa in 2018, requiring sponsorship by an approved employer. Australia relies heavily on skilled migration to fill labour shortages in healthcare, engineering, IT, and construction. The 2023 Migration Strategy Review recommended significant reforms to make Australia's migration system more responsive to skills needs and more humane for international students and temporary residents.
laws.penalty: Working without proper authorization: criminal penalties for workers and employers
exceptions: Working holiday makers (417/462) have work rights with restrictions
Student visa holders can work 48 hours per fortnight during studies

quiz.q: What visa subclass replaced the 457 visa for skilled temporary workers in Australia in 2018?
quiz.explanation: The Temporary Skill Shortage (TSS) visa subclass 482 replaced the 457 visa in March 2018, with stricter requirements for English language ability and work experience, and different streams for short-term and medium-term occupations.

laws.title: Australian Broadcasting Corporation Act 1983
laws.subtitle: ABC independence and public broadcasting
laws.fullDescription: The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) is Australia's public broadcaster, funded by government appropriation (~AU$1.1 billion/year) but required to be editorially independent under its charter. The ABC has faced repeated funding cuts and political attacks — particularly from conservative governments citing perceived 'left bias'. The ABC and SBS (Special Broadcasting Service, Australia's multicultural broadcaster) are central to Australian cultural life.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for broadcasting content (editorial); defamation law applies
exceptions: ABC exempt from some commercial broadcasting obligations
Editorial independence protected in ABC Act

quiz.q: Approximately how much does the Australian government fund the ABC annually?
quiz.explanation: The Australian Broadcasting Corporation receives approximately AU$1.1 billion in annual government appropriation, making it one of the largest public broadcasters relative to population size among comparable democracies.

laws.title: Agricultural Exports / WTO Disputes
laws.subtitle: Farm exports and WTO mechanisms
laws.fullDescription: Agriculture is central to Australia's export economy — beef, wheat, dairy, wool, and horticulture are major exports. The WTO dispute with China over barley tariffs (imposed in 2020) was won by Australia in 2023, with China removing the tariffs. Australia uses WTO dispute mechanisms actively and has been involved in cases against US steel tariffs and Japanese fishing restrictions. Australian agriculture faces increasing biosecurity risks and competition from South American producers.
laws.penalty: Violations of export certification: criminal penalties; fraudulent country-of-origin labeling: significant fines
exceptions: Country-of-origin labeling has 'made in Australia' specific rules
Organic certification has separate accreditation

quiz.q: In which year did Australia win its WTO dispute over China's barley tariffs?
quiz.explanation: Australia won its WTO dispute against China's punitive 80.5% barley tariffs in 2023, with China subsequently removing the tariffs as trade relations began to normalize after the post-COVID diplomatic tensions.

laws.title: Your Future Your Super / Performance Tests
laws.subtitle: Super fund performance and member protection
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Your Future Your Super reforms (2021) introduced annual performance benchmarking of superannuation funds by APRA, publishing results on YourSuper comparison tool. Underperforming funds must notify members. The Stapling of superannuation accounts to individuals (rather than opening new accounts each time they change employer) aims to reduce multiple accounts and fee erosion. Your Super funds manage AU$3.5 trillion for ~16 million Australians.
laws.penalty: Fund trustees failing fiduciary duties: civil penalties; APRA can disqualify trustees
exceptions: Defined benefit schemes have modified performance frameworks
Some industry-specific funds have special parameters

quiz.q: What does 'stapling' of superannuation accounts mean under Australia's 2021 reforms?
options: Merging all super accounts into one government fund
Linking super accounts to individuals so they follow the person between jobs
Requiring employers to match worker super contributions
Fixing super contribution rates for all employers
quiz.explanation: 'Stapling' of superannuation means the account follows the individual between employers, so workers no longer automatically get a new superannuation account each time they change jobs, reducing the number of multiple accounts and the associated fee drain.

laws.title: High Court of Australia / Landmark Cases
laws.subtitle: Constitutional interpretation and judicial review
laws.fullDescription: Australia's High Court, established by the Judicature Act 1903, is the final court of appeal and constitutional arbiter. Landmark decisions include Mabo v Queensland (1992, native title), Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007, prisoners' right to vote), and NZYQ v Minister for Immigration (2023, indefinite detention). The High Court has an originalist but evolving approach to constitutional interpretation and has been willing to strike down legislation that violates implied constitutional rights.
laws.penalty: High Court orders are binding; failure to comply can result in contempt of court
exceptions: Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament can legislate around some HCA rulings
Constitutional amendments can override HCA interpretations

quiz.q: Which 2023 High Court case found that indefinite immigration detention was unconstitutional?
quiz.explanation: The 2023 NZYQ v Minister for Immigration case saw the High Court overturn its 2004 Al-Kateb decision, ruling that indefinite immigration detention is unconstitutional, leading to the release of hundreds of people from immigration detention.

laws.title: Online Gambling Laws / Sports Betting
laws.subtitle: Interactive gambling and harm minimization
laws.fullDescription: The Interactive Gambling Act 2001 prohibits offering most online casino and poker games to Australians, but allows sports betting and lotteries online. Australia has one of the world's highest per-capita gambling losses (~AU$1,600/person/year). Sports betting advertising — particularly live odds during sports broadcasts and use of celebrity endorsements — has been highly controversial. The 2024 review recommended major restrictions on gambling advertising.
laws.penalty: Illegal online gambling services: criminal penalties; licensing violations: significant fines
exceptions: Licensed Australian sports betting services can operate online
Poker machines (pokies) regulated by states/territories

quiz.q: Approximately how much does Australia lose per capita from gambling each year — one of the world's highest rates?
quiz.explanation: Australia has one of the world's highest per-capita gambling losses, with Australians losing approximately AU$1,600 per person per year, driven largely by poker machines (pokies), sports betting, and lottery products.

laws.title: Help to Buy / Affordable Housing
laws.subtitle: Federal housing policy and affordability
laws.fullDescription: Australia's housing affordability crisis has made homeownership increasingly unattainable for young Australians — the median house price in Sydney exceeds AU$1.4 million and Melbourne AU$900,000. The Help to Buy scheme (shared equity with government owning up to 40% of the property) aims to help Australians buy with smaller deposits. The Housing Accord targets 1.2 million new homes by 2029, requiring significant planning reform and construction industry capacity expansion.
laws.penalty: Building Code violations: significant fines; defective buildings: civil liability for builders and certifiers
exceptions: Social housing has separate public funding and management
State-run stamp duty concessions for first-home buyers

quiz.q: What is the approximate target number of new homes under Australia's Housing Accord by 2029?
quiz.explanation: Australia's National Housing Accord targets the construction of 1.2 million new homes between 2024 and 2029, requiring significant state planning reforms, increased construction workforce capacity, and government funding support.
